title: Newton's laws of motion
overview: Apply F = ma to connected particles, pulleys and inclined planes. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Apply Newton's laws to particles of constant mass.
Use W=mg and include friction, tension or thrust correctly.
Solve motion on rough inclines and vertical lines.
Model connected particles with a light inextensible string and smooth pulley.

definitions.definition: The vector sum of all external forces on a body.
For constant mass, resultant force equals ma.
A pulling force transmitted by a taut string.
A string whose mass is neglected, allowing common tension in the ideal model.
A string of fixed length, so connected particles share acceleration magnitude while taut.

sections.title: Applying F=ma
content: Draw a force diagram for one body at a time, choose a positive direction, then write ΣF=ma in that direction. Forces opposite the positive direction enter negatively; acceleration uses the same sign convention.
bullets: F=ma uses resultant force, not any single force.
Equilibrium is the special case a=0.

sections.title: Vertical and inclined motion
content: Resolve weight into mg sinθ along an incline and mg cosθ perpendicular. Friction opposes motion and can make upward and downward accelerations different. In vertical motion, weight remains downward throughout.
bullets: Use R to determine friction where needed.
At a turning point velocity is zero but the force and acceleration need not be.

sections.title: Connected particles
content: For a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley, use one acceleration magnitude and common tension. Write a separate F=ma equation for each particle, then solve simultaneously. A whole-system equation can remove internal tension as a check.
bullets: Do not put forces from two different bodies on one free-body diagram.
Check that a computed tension is non-negative and the string remains taut.

sections.title: Towing and thrust
content: A car and trailer have common acceleration while connected. Treat the tow-bar force as tension if pulling and thrust/compression if pushing. Use the whole system for acceleration, then one body for the connector force.
bullets: Resistance may act separately on each body.
Newton's third-law pair acts on different bodies.

formulas.label: Connected system
formulas.expression: common |a| and common T for a light taut string over a smooth pulley

diagram.title: Newton's laws of motion: revision route

examTips: Use one equation per body and label which body it describes.
Check model assumptions—light string, smooth pulley, taut connection—before equating tensions or accelerations.
Show the mathematical setup and exact working before the final rounded answer; unsupported calculator output may not earn method marks.
commonMistakes: Using F=ma for a single force instead of the resultant.
Giving connected particles opposite signed accelerations after already choosing their separate positive directions inconsistently.
Including an action–reaction pair on the same body.

quickRecall.question: What belongs on the left of F=ma?
quickRecall.answer: The signed resultant of all forces on that one body.

quickRecall.question: Why do ideal connected particles share acceleration magnitude?
quickRecall.answer: The taut string is inextensible, so its length cannot change.

quickRecall.question: How can tension be eliminated?
quickRecall.answer: Apply F=ma to the whole connected system; tension is internal.

quickRecall.question: Can acceleration differ going up and down a rough incline?
quickRecall.answer: Yes, because friction reverses direction while gravity's component does not.
